posts.title: When a Commit and an Email Disagree
posts.summary: Avoid the dual write. Commit the business change and a durable outbox record together, then deliver asynchronously with a stable message identity, idempotent consumers, and an honest at-least-once contract.

posts.title: Revocation Is a Latency Requirement
posts.summary: The useful question is not whether authorization may be cached. It is how long a removed relationship, disabled account, or emergency restriction may still authorize an operation—and whether the full path can prove that bound.

posts.title: What "Cancel" Means After an Agent Starts Work
posts.summary: Model cancellation as a state transition with a final outcome. Stop queued work, propagate cancellation where possible, and reconcile effects already handed to another system.

posts.title: A Page Cursor Is Not Permission to Keep Reading
posts.summary: Treat a page cursor as continuation state, not an access grant. Bind it to the query shape, reject incompatible reuse, and apply fresh authorization before every page.

posts.title: A Date Is Not a Timestamp
posts.summary: Keep civil dates, local date-times, and instants as different types. A bare YYYY-MM-DD should not pass through a timestamp parser merely because both happen to use ISO-looking text.

posts.title: Starting a Job Is Not the Same as Finishing It
posts.summary: A successful call can mean that work was accepted, not that its external effect happened. Model long-running work as an operation with a durable status and make agents distinguish started from completed.

posts.title: Retry Queues Need Deadlines, Not Just Attempt Counts
posts.summary: Attach an expiry to retryable work. The deadline protects systems from turning a temporary dependency failure into stale, surprising side effects.

posts.title: Agent Tool Calls Need Traces, Not Just Logs
posts.summary: Tool logs answer what ran. A trace answers which agent decision caused it, what it waited on, and whether the failure belongs to the model, orchestration, or downstream service.

posts.title: Background Work Needs a Named Owner
posts.summary: Every background task needs a durable identity, a responsible service, a deadline, and a terminal outcome that another system can inspect.

posts.title: Rate Limits Need a Budget the Client Can See
posts.summary: Expose a rate-limit policy and remaining budget deliberately. Clients can then schedule work instead of discovering capacity only by being rejected.

posts.title: An Incident Timeline Needs Two Clocks
posts.summary: Record when an event occurred and when your system learned about it. Delayed delivery, clock skew, and retries make the distinction operationally necessary.

posts.title: Retries Need an Identity Before They Need Backoff
posts.summary: Before tuning retry delays, give each side effect a stable identity. Otherwise a network timeout can become a duplicate charge, email, or deployment.

posts.title: Deadline Budgets Are the Missing Guardrail for AI Agents
posts.summary: If an agent workflow does not carry a deadline budget across tool calls, each hop can wait too long, pile up resources, and amplify outages. Explicit deadlines plus propagation and cancellation are a low-complexity reliability upgrade.

posts.title: Idempotency Keys Are the Seatbelt for AI Agents
posts.summary: Retries are necessary in real systems, but retries plus side effects create duplicate writes, charges, and messages. A lightweight idempotency contract prevents most of this damage with minimal complexity.
